- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.

# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

# LLM-based vs Traditional Static Analysis and Deep Learning Approaches for Source Code Vulnerability Detection: A Comparative Review

- Project id: `2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis`
- Started: 2026-11-12
- Owner: the user (beginner researcher). Claude manages the workflow.

## Topic in plain language
Software vulnerabilities (security bugs such as SQL injection or buffer overflows) are usually found with *static application security testing* (SAST) tools — programs like CodeQL or Semgrep that scan source code with hand-written rules — or with deep-learning (DL) models trained on labelled vulnerable code. Since 2023, large language models (LLMs such as GPT-4, Claude, CodeLlama) are also used to find vulnerabilities, sometimes alone, sometimes combined with SAST. Practitioners and researchers want to know: which approach actually finds more real vulnerabilities, with fewer false alarms, at what cost? Published results disagree, partly because studies use different benchmarks and metrics. This project collects and compares that evidence side by side.

## Scope
- In scope: detection of vulnerabilities in *source code* (any language) by (a) LLMs (prompting, fine-tuning, agentic/reasoning), (b) SAST tools, (c) DL/transformer detectors (e.g. Devign, LineVul), and (d) hybrids of LLM + static analysis; empirical comparisons, benchmarks, and surveys that compare these families.
- Out of scope: binary/malware analysis, fuzzing and dynamic analysis as the main method, vulnerability *repair* only (no detection), network intrusion detection, LLM security itself (jailbreaks, prompt injection).
- Time window (publication years): 2020–2026 (LLM studies mostly 2023+; 2020–2022 only for key DL/SAST baselines and benchmarks).
- Disciplines / venues of interest: software engineering and security (ICSE, FSE, ASE, ISSTA, TSE, TOSEM, USENIX Security, CCS, S&P, IEEE Access, EMSE, IST).
- Target size for the first pass: up to 20 included papers (raise only with a reason).

## Objectives
1. Compare the detection performance (precision, recall, F1, false-positive rate) of LLM-based, SAST and DL approaches as reported in head-to-head studies.
2. Compare *how* they were evaluated (benchmarks, languages, CWE types, data-leakage control, realistic vs. synthetic code) to judge how far the results can be trusted and generalised.
3. Assess whether hybrid LLM + static-analysis designs outperform either family alone, and at what cost (compute, API cost, time).
4. Identify evidence-backed gaps and practical guidance for choosing an approach.

## Inclusion / exclusion criteria
| Include if | Exclude if |
|---|---|
| peer-reviewed journal/conference paper, or a preprint that is highly relevant and flagged as such | not about the topic; no empirical or methodological contribution; retracted; duplicate version |
| empirically evaluates LLM-based source-code vulnerability detection against at least one SAST or DL baseline, OR is a benchmark/dataset study used for such comparisons, OR is a survey/SLR comparing these families | LLM-only evaluation with no baseline (unless a central benchmark/realism study); detection of non-security bugs only; binary code only; repair-only |
| reports quantitative detection metrics or a structured comparison | no quantitative results and no structured comparison; low-quality/predatory venue |

## Search strategy
- Sources: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv (+ PubMed for biomedical topics)
- Query strings (one per facet):
  - F1 head-to-head: "large language model versus static application security testing vulnerability detection"
  - F2 LLM vs DL detectors: "large language model vulnerability detection deep learning baseline LineVul benchmark"
  - F3 hybrids: "LLM static analysis combined vulnerability detection false positive reduction CodeQL"
  - F4 evaluation realism: "vulnerability detection dataset data leakage label noise realistic evaluation PrimeVul"
  - F5 reasoning/agentic: "LLM agent reasoning vulnerability detection evaluation 2025"
  - F6 surveys: "survey large language models software vulnerability detection" 
- Snowballing: references/citations of the most central papers.
- Every executed search is recorded automatically in `search/search-log.md`.

## Key decisions
<!-- Append: date — decision — reason (in plain language). -->
- 2026-11-12 — Topic chosen by user from 4 candidates (LLM vs SAST vulnerability detection) — recent (most work 2025–26), manageable size (~155 title-matching papers since 2023 on OpenAlex), clear comparison axis, high practical value.
- 2026-11-12 — Paper type: comparative literature review (no own experiments) — user choice; easiest to finish while still publishable.
- 2026-11-12 — Defaults: 2020–2026 window, peer-reviewed first, ≤20 included papers; preprints allowed only if central and flagged.
- 2026-11-12 — 20 papers included from 6 facets (3 parallel scouts, ~19 searches, snowballing from PrimeVul, IRIS, zhou2024comparison). VulnLLM-R dropped (preprint without venue) to hold the 20-paper target. IRIS (ICLR 2025) and RepoAudit (ICML 2025) are peer-reviewed although rlab records them as arXiv preprints (those venues issue no DOIs).
# Research questions — LLM-based vs Traditional Static Analysis and Deep Learning Approaches for Source Code Vulnerability Detection: A Comparative Review

<!-- 3-5 questions. Each must be answerable from literature evidence. -->

## RQ1: How do LLM-based approaches compare with SAST tools and DL detectors in detection effectiveness (precision, recall, F1, false-positive rate) in head-to-head evaluations?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: the core practical question — which approach finds more real vulnerabilities with fewer false alarms.
- Linked objective: 1
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11], but CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale general coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++) while most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Versus fine-tuned DL the ranking depends on dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. **Strength: weak–moderate.** Most robust pattern [I]: LLMs have higher recall, lower precision.

## RQ2: How do evaluation setups (benchmarks, languages, CWE coverage, synthetic vs. real-world code, data-leakage control) differ across studies, and how do they explain disagreements in reported results?
- Type: methodological
- Why it matters: results that look contradictory may come from different benchmarks; this decides how much any number can be trusted.
- Linked objective: 2
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: Evaluation setup explains much of the disagreement: label noise (39–65% correct) [@risse2025top, p. 8], exact-copy leakage up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4], balanced vs realistic class ratios that flip rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7], synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5], function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8], and custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. **Strength: moderate–strong** (consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs).

## RQ3: Do hybrid LLM + static-analysis approaches outperform either family alone, and what are the trade-offs in cost, speed and explainability?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: industry is moving to combined tools; evidence for their benefit is scattered.
- Linked objective: 3
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at < $0.20 per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18] (**moderate**). Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12], and needs a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10] (**weak/contested**). LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 per project vs minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Explainability is limited: LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11] and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9].

## RQ4: Which vulnerability types (CWEs), languages and code scales does each family handle well or poorly?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: guides tool choice for a given codebase and points to where research is missing.
- Linked objective: 1, 4
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs and worst on context-dependent and crypto/policy CWEs and on localising memory-safety bugs [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]; CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. 109	- Evidence that the gap exists:
110	  - **Results sit at the flag-everything level.** On 50/50 data, "flag everything" gives F1 0.667. Studies with balanced data report best values at or below that level, and only shu2026evaluating reports the dummy baseline itself:

116	    - shu: fine-tuned GPT-4o wins on balanced data, but PLMs win on the 17%-vulnerable test [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40] [V].
117	    - yildiz: F1 falls from about 49–65 to 5.41–12.21 on non-paired data [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7] [V].
118	  - **Scoring is unequal between families.**
119	    - gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6] [V].
120	    - The CASTLE prompt reveals the scoring scheme to the LLM [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9] [V].
121	    - Statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8] [V].
122	  - **Headline LLM-vs-SAST numbers use five incompatible metrics**: macro F1, CASTLE score, accuracy, detection ratio, recall/SFDR [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @zhou2024comparison, p. 5; @li2026llm, p. 11] [I].

124	    - a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11] [V];
125	    - GPT-4 pairwise correctness is below the 22.70% random reference [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9] [V].
126	  - **Statistics are rare.** Only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count].
127	  - **Authors call for guidelines.** yildiz2025benchmarking calls for evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 2] [A]. ding2025vulnerability proposes VD-S because accuracy and F1 mislead [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2] [A].

129	  - *Pitfalls in Machine Learning for Computer Security* (CACM 2024, doi:10.1145/3643456) and *Pitfalls in LMs for Code Intelligence* (TOSEM 2025, doi:10.1145/3748647): generic pitfall catalogues with no re-scoring of vulnerability-detection results.

131	  - *How much model does warning triage need?* (American Impact Review 2026, doi:10.66308/air.e80134906): re-scores models against a simple reference with MCC and bootstrap CIs, but for actionable-warning triage, not vulnerability detection, and in an unknown-tier venue.
132	  - The CAI 2026 review (doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137) recommends reporting practices but, from its abstract, does not recompute published results.

134	  We found no study that recomputes published LLM, SAST and DL vulnerability-detection results against trivial baselines and realistic prevalence (searches on 2026-11-12).

It also yields a minimal reporting checklist (confusion matrix, prevalence, trivial baselines, unit and location rule, runs/variance).
137	- Suggested study (secondary analysis of published numbers; no model runs):
138	  - **Data:** results tables of the 16 primary studies (plus any added papers). Extract every (study, tool, dataset, configuration) row that reports enough to rebuild a confusion matrix: TP/FP/FN/TN, or P, R and prevalence.
139	  - **Sample:** all extractable rows. Rows without prevalence or FPR are listed separately, not dropped silently.
140	  - **Method:** for each row compute:
141	    - MCC;
142	    - Youden's J = recall − FPR;
143	    - ΔF1 = F1 − F1_flag-all, where F1_flag-all = 2π/(1+π) and π is prevalence;
144	    - precision at deployment prevalence (π = 1%, 5%, 17%) via P = R·π / (R·π + FPR·(1−π)).
145	  - **Baselines:** always-vulnerable; random (P-C reference 22.70% for ding-style pairs); published dummy or word-count baselines where available.
146	  - **Analysis:** within each study, rank tools before and after re-scoring and count rank reversals (Kendall τ). Do not pool across datasets marked "not comparable" in methodology comparison §3. Report how many rows fail to beat flag-all.
147	  - **Threats:** many rows lack TN/FPR (selection bias); rounding in published tables; lenient TP definitions cannot be undone after the fact; transcription errors (mitigate by double extraction and spot-checking against PDFs).
148	- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy**. Needs only a spreadsheet or about 50 lines of Python, no GPU and no API cost, and takes about 2–4 weeks. It can be included directly in the comparative review as an added-value table.
149	
150	## G2: No same-benchmark, leakage-controlled comparison of LLMs vs SAST vs fine-tuned DL on real, post-cutoff code
151	- Gap type: evidence / methodological
152	- Evidence that the gap exists:
153	  - **Only one study runs all three families, and its SAST arm is synthetic.** khare2025understanding is the only study that evaluates LLMs, SAST and DL, and CodeQL runs on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7] [V].
154	  - **zhou2024comparison has no classic DL detector.** It compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4] [V].
155	  - **Studies that call for this comparison:**
156	    - chakraborty2024revisiting: evaluate static and dynamic analysis tools on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13] [A];
157	    - ding2025vulnerability: hybrid LM + program-analysis systems [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 10] [A].
158	  - **Results reverse across setups.**
159	    - LLM vs SAST rankings reverse between small programs, synthetic suites and repositories [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @li2026llm, p. 7] [V].
160	    - LLM vs DL rankings reverse with dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40] [V].
161	  - **Contamination and leakage are rarely controlled.**
162	    - Exact-copy leakage reaches up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] [V].
163	    - Benchmarks are probably in pre-training data [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 30] [A], and post-cutoff datasets are recommended [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 38] [A].
164	    - Only xiong2026sifting and li2026llm test on post-cutoff code [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5] [V].
165	  - **Survey future work asks only for verified benchmarks.** The surveys' future directions call for verified, contamination-free, repository-level benchmarks [@zhou2025large, p. 22; @sheng2025llms, p. 25] [A], but not for a controlled three-family comparison [I].
166	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q6, Q7, Q8 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025; contamination angle Q19, Q20; W3, W6). Closest hits, each missing at least one family:
167	  - *From Lab to Reality* (arXiv 2512.10485, accepted at JSS): DL detectors and four open LLMs on VentiVul, a temporally separated set of 200 recent Linux/Chromium vulnerabilities. **No SAST arm.**
168	  - *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026, doi:10.3390/computers15090623): eight LLMs vs a fine-tuned 125M detector on label-clean PrimeVul, reporting precision at 1:44 prevalence. **No SAST; not post-cutoff by design.**
169	  - *A Real CVE-Backed Benchmark for WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Detection* (BDCC 2026, doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303): a static taint analyser plus ML/DL under plugin-grouped, de-duplicated CV. **No LLM.**
170	  - *RealVuln* (arXiv 2604.13764): SAST vs LLMs vs specialised scanners on 26 intentionally vulnerable Python repositories. **No DL; not real-world CVEs; the authors' company product is evaluated.**
171	  - *A Comparative Evaluation of LLMs for Real-World Vulnerability Detection: Big-Vul and CVEfixes* (IJANSER 2026, OpenAlex W7218261049): LLMs vs static baselines on balanced Big-Vul/CVEfixes. **No DL; noisy, non-post-cutoff data.**
172	  - *VulEval* (arXiv 2404.15596, reportedly TSE 2026): repository-level evaluation of DL and LLM methods. From its abstract, no SAST arm.
173	  - Contamination studies of LLM-only detection, which leave the cross-family comparison open:
174	    - CWE-Trace (arXiv 2606.20502);
175	    - BenchGuard (LNCS 2026, doi:10.1007/978-3-032-33260-8_22);
176	    - the ASE 2025 industry-showcase paper "Should We Evaluate LLM Based Security Analysis Approaches on Open Source Systems" (no identifier returned).
177	
178	  We found no study that runs SAST, fine-tuned DL and LLMs on the same real-world, de-duplicated, post-cutoff targets with a shared unit and metric (searches on 2026-11-12).
179	- Confidence: **medium**. Many near misses each lack exactly one family, so a paper filling the gap could appear soon. Re-check before submission.
180	- Potential contribution: the first like-for-like answer to RQ1 on realistic code, and an estimate of how much of the LLM advantage is due to contamination (pre- vs post-cutoff subsets). This also absorbs candidate gap 7 (contamination).
181	- Suggested study:
182	  - **Data:** Python (build-free for SAST) or Java CVEs. Collect vulnerability-fixing commits from GitHub Security Advisories/OSV (CVEfixes or MoreFixes pipeline). Split into a *post-cutoff* set (disclosed after the newest evaluated model's training cutoff) and a *pre-cutoff* set of the same size.
183	  - **Sample:** about 100 post-cutoff and 100 pre-cutoff CVEs. Use the vulnerable function before the fix plus its patched version (pairs), and add non-changed functions from the same files to reach a realistic ratio (e.g. 1:20). Manually verify a random 50 positives (two raters, Cohen's κ), as in risse2025top.
184	  - **Arms:**
185	    - SAST: Semgrep (security rulesets) and CodeQL `security-extended`, default and tuned query suites.
186	    - DL: UniXcoder or CodeBERT fine-tuned on pre-cutoff data with project-disjoint splits.
187	    - LLM: 2–3 open 7–14B models (local) and optionally one API model, zero-shot and chain-of-thought, 3 runs each.
188	  - **Unit mapping:** a SAST warning counts for the function that contains its line. Also report file-level results so that SAST is not penalised by the mapping.
189	  - **Metrics:** recall, precision and MCC at the natural ratio; pairwise correctness on pairs; flag rate; cost (USD, GPU-hours, wall time).
190	  - **Baselines:** flag-all, random, and a function-length classifier (the WordPress study found it competitive).
191	  - **Analysis:** McNemar tests between arms on identical functions; project-level bootstrap CIs; pre- vs post-cutoff difference per arm as a contamination estimate.
192	  - **Threats:**
193	    - noisy fix-commit labels;
194	    - function mapping disadvantages SAST;
195	    - small fine-tuning data for Python;
196	    - prompt sensitivity;
197	    - residual contamination (advisories published before the CVE date);
198	    - limited generalisation beyond one language.
199	- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. All tools are free, and a 7B model runs on Colab or a laptop GPU. The hard parts are dataset construction and mapping warnings to functions. Expect 6–10 weeks. A low-cost variant reuses VentiVul (from *From Lab to Reality*) and adds only the SAST arm, but C/C++ requires compiling for CodeQL.
200	
201	## G3: True-positive loss in LLM filtering of SAST alarms is not controlled per CWE on real security alerts
202	- Gap type: practical / methodological
203	- Evidence that the gap exists:
204	  - **xiong2026sifting.** The best agent configuration cuts OWASP FPR from 98.3% to 6.3% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12] but drops 22.25% of true vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
205	    - The miss rate is low for injection CWEs (CWE-78 2.38%, CWE-89 1.10%, CWE-79 0.41%) [V].
206	    - It is 77.17% for weak cryptography and 84.50% for weak hashing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
207	    - The authors plan "CWE-aware, cost-adaptive agent strategies and human-in-the-loop" auditing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A].
208	  - **du2026reducing.** Removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall of 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8] [V]. This covers non-security bug types and the authors' own method.
209	  - **Recommended but not evaluated.** kaniewski2026systematic recommends SAST → LLM false-positive filtering pipelines [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 42] [A] but its corpus excludes them [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8].
210	  - **Real-world samples are small.** xiong uses 50 alerts per set [@xiong2026sifting, p. 13] [V].
211	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q13, Q14, Q24 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025, plus Q25; W5). Closest hits, all not analysed:
212	  - *ZeroFalse* (arXiv 2510.02534): CWE-specific context, high F1 on OWASP/OpenVuln, claims to preserve coverage.
213	  - *Using LLMs to Adjudicate Static-Analysis Alerts with Error Reduction Techniques* (arXiv 2607.09979): consistency checks reach ≥98% recall on Juliet, FormAI and SV-COMP, which are synthetic suites.
214	  - *QASecClaw* (arXiv 2605.01885): multi-agent FP reduction on OWASP.
215	  - *Case-Level Verification in Scanner-LLM Cascades* (arXiv 2610.08406): formalises the FP-reduction vs TPR trade-off, but for DAST.
216	  - *Trusting the Tool* (arXiv 2610.32876): false analyser assurances lower detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points.
217	
218	  These show that TP loss is being measured, and can be reduced on synthetic suites. We found no study that tests a CWE-aware selective filtering policy, i.e. one that filters only CWE classes with demonstrated low miss rates, with held-out evaluation and full FP-reduction vs TP-retention curves on real-world security alerts (searches on 2026-11-12).
219	- Confidence: **low–medium**. This is an active area with many 2025–26 preprints. The gap is narrow and could be filled quickly.
220	- Potential contribution: an operating-point view of alarm filtering, i.e. what share of real vulnerabilities is lost per CWE for a given FP reduction. Also a simple routing policy that practitioners can adopt.
221	- Suggested study:
222	  - **Data:**
223	    - OWASP Benchmark v1.2 (Java, 2,740 labelled cases, official scorer) for development.
224	    - A real-world set of about 100 SAST alerts from post-cutoff open-source Java projects, labelled by two raters (κ), for testing.
225	  - **Method:** run Semgrep and CodeQL; ask 2 open LLMs (7–8B) for a TP/FP verdict with a confidence score, 3 runs.
226	  - **Policies:**
227	    - no filter;
228	    - filter-all (xiong's vanilla);
229	    - CWE-aware filter that applies the LLM only to CWEs whose miss rate was below 5% on a development half of OWASP, evaluated on the other half and on the real set.
230	  - **Metrics:** FP-reduction rate; TP retention; residual FPR; expected triage cost = c_FP·FP + c_FN·FN for cost ratios 1:10 to 1:100.
231	  - **Analysis:** curves across confidence thresholds; per-CWE bootstrap CIs.
232	  - **Threats:** OWASP is synthetic and probably in pre-training data; per-CWE cells are small; rater bias.
233	- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy–moderate**. Ground truth and the scorer are public, Java SAST on OWASP builds easily, and 7B models run locally. Expect 4–6 weeks. The main effort is labelling the real-world alerts.
234	
235	## G4: Hybrid LLM+SAST detectors lack independent replication that separates target, metric and labeller effects
236	- Gap type: contradiction / evidence
237	- Evidence that the gap exists:
238	  - **RepoAudit: author evaluation vs independent evaluation.**
239	    - Authors: 78.43% precision and all 21 known bugs reproduced, one run per setting [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 17] [V].
240	    - Independent (li2026llm): 0 of 110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities and 92.77% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11] [V]; cost up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
241	  - **IRIS: author evaluation vs independent evaluation.**
242	    - Authors: 55 vs 27 of 120 CVEs detected compared with CodeQL [@li2024iris, p. 8] [V].
243	    - Independent: 97.80% vs 77.00% SFDR on new Java projects [@li2026llm, p. 12] [V].
244	  - **The independent study labels with an LLM it also evaluates.** li2026llm labels warnings with Codex, which it also evaluates [@li2026llm, p. 11] [V], so its labeller is not independent [I].
245	  - **The gain depends on a strong LLM.** IRIS gains depend on GPT-4; smaller LLMs worsen FDR [@li2024iris, p. 10] [V].
246	  - **Neither paper settles the discrepancy** (methodology comparison §4, C2/C6) [I].
247	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q11, Q12, Q23 on arXiv/OpenAlex/Crossref from 2024/2025; W3). Closest hits:
248	  - li2026llm (in corpus) is itself the only independent re-evaluation.
249	  - *What Survives the Next Model?* (arXiv 2609.00468): re-runs ICSE 2026 technique papers against single prompts, across SE tasks generally.
250	  - *Trusting the Tool* (arXiv 2610.32876): studies LLM deference to analyser evidence, not tool replication.
251	  - Agent tools found (Revelio arXiv 2606.22263, AnyPoC arXiv 2604.11950) are new tools, not replications.
252	
253	  We found no study that re-runs IRIS or RepoAudit on the authors' original benchmark and on new targets, under the same blinded human labelling, so that the discrepancy can be attributed (searches on 2026-11-12).
254	- Confidence: **medium**. Reproductions may exist in artifact-evaluation reports that are not indexed.
255	- Potential contribution: tells practitioners whether published hybrid gains transfer to new code. It also tells researchers which evaluation choices (targets, metric, labeller, model version) drive the reported differences.
256	- Suggested study:
257	  - **Design:** 2 × 2 factorial — target set (original CWE-Bench-Java subset vs post-cutoff Java CVEs) × metric (the original "detected CVE" metric vs sampled false-discovery rate), on the **same** runs.
258	  - **Data:** 30 CWE-Bench-Java CVEs across 4 CWEs, plus 10–15 post-cutoff Java CVEs. IRIS code and data are public [@li2024iris, p. 2].
259	  - **Arms:** IRIS with the original LLM family where affordable, and with one open model; CodeQL alone as baseline.
260	  - **Labelling:** a random sample of ≥100 warnings labelled by two humans blinded to the tool (κ reported).
261	  - **Metrics:** detections, FDR/SFDR, cost (tokens, USD, time).
262	  - **Threats:** model deprecation (GPT-4 versions); CodeQL version drift; build failures; API cost.
263	- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate–hard**. Building Java projects for CodeQL and running a hybrid pipeline is demanding. A reduced IRIS-only replication on 20–30 CVEs with an open model is feasible in about 8 weeks. RepoAudit (C/C++, high token cost) is not recommended for a beginner.
264	
265	## G5: Repository-level, real-CVE LLM-vs-SAST evidence is missing for PHP, Go and JavaScript (Python only partly covered)
266	- Gap type: population/context
267	- Evidence that the gap exists:
268	  - **The literature is concentrated on C/C++ and Java.**
269	    - Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28] [V].
270	    - 555 mappable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 34] [V].
271	    - Directions call for Python, Java, Rust and multilingual benchmarks [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 40] [A].
272	  - **Authors list other languages as future work:**
273	    - RepoAudit: extension to Python and JavaScript [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 10] [A];
274	    - IRIS: other languages [@li2024iris, p. 10] [A];
275	    - du2026reducing: more languages [@du2026reducing, p. 10] [A];
276	    - xiong2026sifting: more languages and SAST tools [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A];
277	    - li2026llm: broader languages and CWE classes [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A].
278	  - **The few multi-language studies are thin or lack SAST.**
279	    - The only multi-language LLM study (REEF, 7 languages) has no SAST arm [@shu2026evaluating, p. 7] [V].
280	    - zhou2024comparison covers Python with roughly 8–10 test CVEs per language [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6] [I].
281	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q17, Q18, Q26 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025; W8). Closest hits:
282	  - *RealVuln* (arXiv 2604.13764): Python, but intentionally vulnerable repositories and a vendor author.
283	  - JavaScript:
284	    - *LLMs Cannot Reliably Detect Vulnerabilities in JavaScript* (arXiv 2512.01255): LLM-focused benchmark;
285	    - *Exploring Automated Vulnerability Identification in JavaScript Code Using LLMs* (arXiv 2609.13816): snippet-level, LLM vs SAST.
286	  - PHP: *WordPress plugin benchmark* (doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303): a static taint analyser vs ML/DL, no LLM. The taint analyser misses about 98% of vulnerabilities (abstract only).
287	  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): LLMs only, C/C++/Python.
288	  - *A Preliminary Study of LLMs for Multilingual Vulnerability Detection* (ISSTA companion 2025, doi:10.1145/3713081.3731746): PLMs vs LLMs, no SAST.
289	
290	  We found no study comparing LLMs with SAST on real CVEs at repository level for PHP or Go, and only snippet-level or synthetic-repository evidence for JavaScript and Python (searches on 2026-11-12).
291	- Confidence: **low–medium**. Python and JavaScript are being filled quickly. The gap is clearest for PHP and Go.
292	- Potential contribution: tests whether the "LLM higher recall, lower precision" pattern holds in web languages, where injection CWEs (which LLMs handle best [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18]) dominate.
293	- Suggested study:
294	  - **Data:** about 60 real PHP CVEs (e.g. from the released WordPress-plugin benchmark data) or Go CVEs from the Go vulnerability database (OSV).
295	  - **Arms:** Semgrep (supports both languages), a language-specific SAST tool, and 2 open LLMs at file level with retrieved callers. Check CodeQL's supported-language list for the chosen language before planning a CodeQL arm.
296	  - **Metrics:** recall on known CVEs; precision on a manually labelled warning sample; cost.
297	  - **Analysis:** per-CWE recall with CIs.
298	  - **Threats:** label quality (the WordPress paper finds 48.8% of cleaned positives genuine, abstract only); small samples; tool coverage differences.
299	- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. The tools are free and build-free for PHP and Go. The main cost is manual labelling of warnings.
300	
301	## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison across LLM, SAST and DL including human triage effort
302	- Gap type: practical
303	- Evidence that the gap exists:
304	  - **Most studies report no monetary cost.** Ten of 16 primary studies report none [I, our count]. The six that do are du, guo, li2026llm, shu, tan and xiong [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16; @shu2026evaluating, p. 42; @tan2026think, p. 10; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17].
305	  - **Where measured, cost is decisive.**
306	    - Per project: from $2.54 in the RepoAudit paper to $172.77 on average and $1,247.66 at most in li2026llm [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
307	    - Thinking mode costs 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 10] [V].
308	  - **Cost is not linked to triage effort.** None of the cost figures is expressed per confirmed true positive, including the analyst time spent on false warnings [I]. li2026llm calls for cost-aware designs [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A].
309	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q15, Q16, Q25 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025; W7). Closest hits:
310	  - *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026, doi:10.3390/computers15090623): measures cost and energy for 8 LLMs vs a fine-tuned detector, with precision at 1:44 prevalence. **No SAST, no triage effort.** This narrows the gap considerably.
311	  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): cost per LLM configuration only.
312	  - Vendor blogs (Semgrep, Endor Labs) report cost per true positive for their own products; these are not peer-reviewed and have conflicts of interest.
313	
314	  We found no peer-reviewed study reporting cost per confirmed vulnerability, including triage time, for all three families on the same targets (searches on 2026-11-12).
315	- Confidence: **low–medium**. The gap is narrowed by *Open or Frontier?*. What remains is the SAST arm and the triage-effort term.
316	- Potential contribution: a decision-oriented metric for practitioners: dollars and analyst minutes per real vulnerability found.
317	- Suggested study: measure as a secondary outcome of G2 (same targets). Record compute cost per arm, then time two raters triaging a random 50 warnings per arm. Cost per TP = (compute + triage minutes × hourly rate) / confirmed TPs, reported with sensitivity bands for hourly rates. Threats: triage time depends on rater skill; API price changes.
318	- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. It is cheap if added to G2, but on its own it needs the same infrastructure.
319	
320	---
321	
322	## Dropped or merged candidates
323	
324	- **Contamination control as a standalone gap (candidate 7)**: *narrowed and merged into G2.* Several LLM-only studies now address it:
325	  - CWE-Trace (arXiv 2606.20502) reports no measurable contamination advantage on Linux-kernel samples (abstract only);
326	  - BenchGuard (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-33260-8_22);
327	  - *Are LLMs Memorizing Bug Benchmarks?* (doi:10.1109/llm4code66737.2025.00005);
328	  - the ASE 2025 industry paper.
329	
330	  What remains open is the comparative question (does the LLM advantage over SAST/DL survive post-cutoff?), which G2 tests via pre- vs post-cutoff subsets. Searches: Q19, Q20, W6.
331	- **Independent labelling, LLM-as-labeller and single runs (W3, W5)**: *merged* into G1 (protocol) and G4 (blinded human labelling). No separate novelty check was run, so they are not reported as separate gaps.
332	- **Statement-level / location-aware scoring**: *merged* into G1. Evidence: [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8; @gnieciak2025large, p. 6].
333	- **Workflow / IDE integration**: *not reported.* It is supported by one survey only [@zhou2025large, p. 19], no dedicated three-query novelty check was run, and Q14 surfaced a pilot human study of LLM-augmented SAST reports (doi:10.1109/csr69374.2026.11759919). It needs developer participants and is a poor fit for a beginner.
334	- **"Does reasoning reduce false positives?" (contradiction C4)**: *not reported as a gap.* tan2026think already provides a controlled factorial test within the corpus [@tan2026think, p. 6], so it is not a gap. The conflicting evidence belongs in the review's discussion, not in this report.
335	
336	## Recommended for inclusion (not added; not analysed)
337	
338	The project target is ≤20 papers, so the orchestrator decides. These are listed by value to RQ1–RQ3 and positioning:
339	1. **arXiv 2512.10485**, *From Lab to Reality* (accepted JSS). DL vs open LLMs on a temporally separated out-of-distribution set. Closest primary study to G2; strengthens RQ1/RQ2.
340	2. **doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303**, *WordPress plugin benchmark* (BDCC 2026). Leakage-controlled static vs learning-based detectors on PHP. Its conclusion that label quality outweighs family differences directly supports our RQ2 thesis, and it adds a non-C/Java language.
341	3. **doi:10.3390/computers15090623**, *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026). Cost and energy for LLMs vs a fine-tuned small detector at realistic prevalence; fills part of W6 and RQ3 cost.
342	4. **doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137**, CAI 2026 review. Closest competing review; must be read and cited in the positioning/related-work section.
343	5. **doi:10.5070/sr3.62177**, [SoK] *LLMs in Security Code Review and Testing* (J. Systems Research 2026). Second positioning competitor (LLM vs traditional tools).
344	6. **arXiv 2604.13764**, *RealVuln* (preprint; authors evaluate their own company's scanner). SAST vs LLM on Python repositories; adds language coverage. Flag the preprint status and conflict of interest.
345	7. Optional, for the RQ3 hybrid and filtering discussion: **arXiv 2510.02534** (ZeroFalse) and **arXiv 2610.32876** (*Trusting the Tool*, Oct 2026), both preprints. Optional, for RQ2: **arXiv 2507.21817** (*Out of Distribution, Out of Luck*, ICSE 2026).

<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). Full discussion: reports/methodology-comparison.md §4. -->
- **C1 Fine-tuned vs GPT-4.** Fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far exceed prompted gpt-4 (29%) on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4], but GPT-4 CoT beats every fine-tuned model on pair-wise correctness on 564 PrimeVul pairs (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. Differs in metric (F1 vs P-C), data (noisy random-split Big-Vul 1:20 vs de-duplicated time-split pairs) and model versions; Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. [I] Fine-tuned models exploit dataset artefacts rewarded by random splits [@risse2025top, p. 11]; on pairs all are below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family.
- **C2 RepoAudit.** Own paper: 40 TP / 11 FP (78.43% precision), all 21 known bugs reproduced, $2.54 and 0.44 h per project [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8]. Independent study: 0/110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7], 92.77% SFDR on real-world projects [@li2026llm, p. 11], average $172.77 per project, max $1,247.66 [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Differs in targets (prior tools' bug reports vs ReposVul CVEs), version (old commits vs current HEAD; the 5 overlapping modules only in li's real-world set), metric (precision vs recall/SFDR), labeller (authors vs Codex), bug types and scale. [I] Dependence on source/sink API coverage (zero-token runs; API modelling explains 108/108 misses [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]). Unresolved.
- **C3 LLM vs SAST.** LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; at repository level LLMs detect more but flag up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint), and general agents lead recall while specialised LLM detectors and SAST show near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Differs in language, unit, synthetic vs real code, and scoring leniency (location rule only for LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; CASTLE prompt reveals scoring [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]). [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, small programs fit LLM context, real repositories defeat both: no single winner.
- **C4 Does reasoning reduce false positives?** For: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]; RepoAudit precision 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against: DeepSeek R1 166 FP vs GPT-4o 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; thinking raises F1 via recall with unchanged accuracy and turns negative under DA/MA [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8]; reasoning LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37]. [I] Holds for OpenAI o-series in some settings only.
- **C5 Class balance flips rankings.** Balanced REEF: fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]; imbalanced test: PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. yildiz F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging; balanced rankings do not transfer to deployment.
- **C6 IRIS hybrid.** IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8], but on real-world Java IRIS SFDR is 97.80% vs CodeQL 77.00% [@li2026llm, p. 12]. Not like-for-like (known CVEs vs new code; detections vs SFDR; labelling). [I] Hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen code. Open.

## Agreements / converging evidence
- **G1 Realistic evaluation collapses performance (strong).** DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]; code-LM F1 62.88–68.26% → 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; LLM accuracy 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic [@khare2025understanding, p. 5]; line-level F1 0.6641 → 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39]; statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8]. Surveys concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20].
- **G2 Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Independent audits: 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8]; 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; ReVeal 15% inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. (The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al. via Ding — not independent.)
- **G3 Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).** GPT-4 two-shot labels both pair members vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; "both vulnerable" is 40–95% of failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8]; dual-agent flags 88.2% [@tan2026think, p. 7]; always-vulnerable rows among khare's best F1 [@khare2025understanding, p. 16]. Partly one dataset family (PrimeVul).
- **G4 SAST recall is low on real code, high only on synthetic suites (moderate).** Best single tools 30.0–44.4%, many 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6]; CodeQL recall 6.00–34.29% C/C++ and 14.19% Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]; CodeQL 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8]; CASTLE CodeQL 29%, SAST average 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12]; vs CodeQL accuracy 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **G5 CodeQL on OWASP replicates across groups (moderate).** P 0.58 / R 0.96 / F1 0.72 [@khare2025understanding, p. 9] vs P 60.3% / R 97.0% / F1 74.4% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 11].
- **G6 Missing context is the shared failure cause (moderate).** All 151 truly vulnerable audited functions need external context [@risse2025top, p. 9]; context-type identification ≤41.33% [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 9]; API modelling explains 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses [@li2026llm, p. 7]; 14.60% of FPs from truncated inter-procedural context [@li2026llm, p. 15].
- **G7 LLM filtering of SAST alarms trades large FP reduction for lost true positives (moderate).** du2026reducing removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8] (own method, Tencent authors, non-security bugs); xiong2026sifting FPR 6.3% with 22.25% miss rate [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18].
- **G8 Prompt-only LLMs trail adapted models (moderate).** Fine-tuned models beat prompted ChatGPT on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]; GPT-3.5 prompting detects 3.7–23.2% vs 89.2% fine-tuned CodeBERT [@zhou2024comparison, p. 10]; prompt-only LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- **G9 LLM cost far exceeds SAST and varies by orders of magnitude (moderate).** RepoAudit averages $172.77 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]; alarm filtering < $0.20 per alarm [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17]; GPT-4o instruction tuning ~15× a PLM run [@shu2026evaluating, p. 42].

49	
50	**A. Head-to-head LLM vs SAST.** Results depend on the unit of analysis. On small, self-contained targets, prompted frontier LLMs score above SAST: macro F1 0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55 on C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]; CASTLE score 977 for GPT-o3-mini vs 661 for the best non-LLM tool [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. On function-level synthetic suites, CodeQL has higher accuracy than the best LLM on all three datasets [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At repository level, LLMs detect more CVEs but mark up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7]. General coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]. [I] The family's main weakness is that each study uses its own targets and scoring, so the papers measure different things (see §3.5).
51	
52	**B. LLM vs fine-tuned DL/PLM.** On random-split Big-Vul, fine-tuned small models clearly beat prompted ChatGPT (F1 94% vs 29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]. Under realistic splits all models collapse [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]. The only multilingual comparison finds that the winner depends on class balance [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. [I] This family inherits the label noise and leakage of Big-Vul-type data (§5, W2).
53	
54	**C1. Hybrid detection (LLM inside the analyser).** IRIS doubles CodeQL's detections on CWE-Bench-Java (55 vs 27 of 120), with AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03% [@li2024iris, p. 8]. Only GPT-4 lowers FDR below CodeQL; smaller LLMs worsen it [@li2024iris, p. 10]. RepoAudit reports 78.43% precision [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 8]. Both look much weaker in li2026llm's independent re-evaluation (§4, C2 and C6).
55	
56	**C2. Hybrid false-positive filtering.** The industrial LLM4PFA hybrid removes 94–98% of false alarms while keeping 75–88% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8]. The best agent configuration cuts OWASP FPR from 98.3% to 6.3% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12] but drops 22.25% of true vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. [I] This is the most consistent benefit in the corpus, but it is a trade-off, not a free gain (§3.7).
57	
58	**D. Agentic/reasoning LLMs.** Thinking mode raises F1 mainly through recall (0.31 → 0.41) at 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 10]. A four-call self-revision matches the multi-agent pipeline on P-C, so much of the agent gain is extra inference budget [@tan2026think, p. 11] [A]. ReAct agents give the best pairwise accuracy with GPT-4o models, but it stays ≤20.17% [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].
59	
60	**E. Benchmark realism.** Manual audits find only 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct in BigVul, Devign and DiverseVul [@risse2025top, p. 8], and 24–36% in CodeXGLUE/Devign and VulnPatchPairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. A word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11]. Statement-level scoring halves LLM F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].
61	
62	**F. Surveys.** Two SLRs and one narrative survey describe a field dominated by function-level C/C++ classification on noisy datasets [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 26; @zhou2025large, p. 18; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. None pools effect sizes. kaniewski2026systematic excludes studies that only post-process tool output [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8], so it does not cover family C2.

100	### 3.7 Agreements / converging evidence
101	
102	- **G1. Realistic evaluation collapses reported performance (strong).** Several studies show it:
103	  - DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7].
104	  - Code-LM F1 falls from 62.88–68.26% (BigVul) to 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
105	  - LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic data [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
106	  - GPT-4o line-level F1 drops from 0.6641 to 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].
107	  - Statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].
108	
109	  The surveys agree [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20].
110	- **G2. Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Two independent audits find 39–65% [@risse2025top, p. 8] and 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] of vulnerable labels correct. ReVeal has 15% label inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al.'s, reproduced by Ding [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; it is not an independent estimate.
111	- **G3. Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).**
112	  - GPT-4 two-shot calls both versions vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
113	  - "Both vulnerable" accounts for 40–95% of LLM failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8].
114	  - The dual-agent design flags 88.2% of functions [@tan2026think, p. 7].
115	  - Several of khare's best F1 rows are "always vulnerable" outputs [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].
116	  - Frontier models over-flag CWE-476/416/190 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13] [A].
117	
118	  [I] ding, yildiz and tan share PrimeVul, so this is partly one dataset family.
119	- **G4. SAST recall is low on real code and high only on synthetic suites (moderate).** On real code:
120	  - Best single SAST tools detect 30.0–44.4% of CVEs, and many detect 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6].
121	  - CodeQL recall is 6.00–34.29% on C/C++ and 14.19% on Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9].
122	  - CodeQL finds 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8].
123	  - On CASTLE, CodeQL reaches 29% and the SAST average is 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12].
124	
125	  On synthetic suites, CodeQL reaches accuracy 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
126	- **G5. Missing context is the shared failure cause (moderate).**
127	  - All 151 truly vulnerable audited functions need context beyond the function [@risse2025top, p. 9].
128	  - LLMs identify required context in ≤41.33% of cases per context type [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 9].

138	## 4. Contradictions
139	
140	**C1. Fine-tuned models vs GPT-4: fu2023chatgpt vs ding2025vulnerability.**
141	- Claim A: fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far outperform prompted gpt-4 (29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4].
142	- Claim B: GPT-4 CoT has a higher P-C (12.94%) than every fine-tuned model (≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
143	- Differences:
144	  - metric: F1 vs pairwise correctness;
145	  - data: noisy random-split Big-Vul at 1:20 vs de-duplicated, time-split PrimeVul pairs;
146	  - time: 2023 vs 2024 GPT versions.
147	- Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu's direction [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
148	- [I] Explanation: fine-tuned models probably exploit dataset artefacts that random splits reward and paired, de-duplicated tests remove [@risse2025top, p. 11]. On pairs, every model is below the random reference (22.70%), so neither side shows real detection skill there, and the reversal says more about the benchmark than about the model families.
149	
150	**C2. RepoAudit: guo2025repoaudit vs li2026llm.**
151	- Claim A: 40 TP / 11 FP (78.43% precision) on 15 C/C++ projects, all 21 known bugs reproduced, $2.54 and 0.44 h per project [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8].
152	- Claim B: in li2026llm, RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) detects 0 of 110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7]. On real projects it has 92.77% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 11] and costs $172.77 on average, up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16].
153	- Differences:
154	  - targets: prior tools' bug reports vs ReposVul CVEs;
155	  - code version: older commits vs current HEAD (the five overlapping Linux/ImageMagick modules are in li's real-world set only);
156	  - metric: precision on own reports vs recall/SFDR;
157	  - labeller: authors vs Codex;
158	  - scale: avg 251 KLoC vs multi-million-LOC modules.
159	- [I] Explanation: RepoAudit depends on source/sink API coverage. li2026llm records zero-token runs and 108/108 misses due to API modelling [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16], so the tool may perform well only on targets matching its built-in specifications. Neither paper alone settles this.
160	
161	**C3. "LLMs beat SAST" vs "SAST beats LLMs" vs repository level.**
162	- Claim A: LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and on CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
163	- Claim B: CodeQL beats the best LLM in accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
164	- Claim C (repository level): LLMs detect more but mark up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7]. General agents reach the highest recall, while specialised LLM detectors and SAST both have near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11].
165	- Differences: language (C#, C, Java), unit (project, program, function, repository), scoring (lenient LLM location rule in gnieciak [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; the CASTLE prompt reveals the scoring rule to the LLM [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]), and synthetic vs real code.
166	- [I] Explanation: synthetic suites match SAST rule sets, while small self-contained programs fit inside an LLM's context. Real repositories defeat both families through missing API and context models (G4, G5). The answer depends on setting and metric, so there is no single winner.
167	
168	**C4. Does reasoning reduce false positives?**
169	- Claim A: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]. RepoAudit precision rises to 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16].
170	- Claim B:
171	  - In CASTLE's own table, DeepSeek R1 has 166 FP vs GPT-4o's 116 [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
172	  - Thinking mode raises F1 through recall with unchanged accuracy, and its F1 benefit turns negative under dual- and multi-agent designs [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8].
173	  - Reasoning LLMs are near chance on REEF (Acc 0.52–0.53) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37].
174	- Differences: OpenAI o-series vs open reasoning models; micro-benchmark and repository agent vs balanced function pairs; FP count vs F1 and accuracy.
175	- [I] Explanation: the claim holds for some proprietary reasoning models in some settings and does not generalise to "reasoning" as such.
176	
177	**C5. Class balance flips the ranking (shu2026evaluating, internal).**
178	- Claim A: on balanced REEF, fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037; MCC 0.4360 vs 0.2860) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
179	- Claim B: on the imbalanced (~17% vulnerable) test, PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626, CodeT5P MCC 0.3627 vs GPT-4o F1 0.4010, MCC 0.2774) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41].
180	- yildiz shows the same sensitivity: F1 falls from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
181	- [I] Explanation: LLMs flag positives more liberally, which balanced sets reward. Rankings from balanced benchmarks should not be carried over to deployment, where vulnerable code is rare.
182	
183	**C6. Hybrid IRIS: original vs independent evaluation.**
184	- Claim A: IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27 detected; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8].
185	- Claim B: on 15 real-world Java projects, IRIS (GPT-4) has 97.80% SFDR vs 77.00% for CodeQL [@li2026llm, p. 12].
186	- Differences: known CVEs vs new code, detections vs SFDR, CodeQL-protocol FDR vs Codex-labelled sampling.
187	- [I] Explanation: hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen projects. The comparison is not like-for-like, so the tension stays open.
188	
189	## 5. Methodological weaknesses across the field
190	
191	- **W1. F1 on balanced data without a trivial baseline.** On a 50/50 set, "flag everything" scores F1 0.667. Examples:
192	  - shu's DummyClf_vul scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
193	  - tan's best F1 is 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7; @tan2026think, p. 11].
194	  - All of yildiz's GPT F1 values (48–66) are at or below it [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6].
195	  - khare's best-per-dataset F1s include always-vulnerable rows [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].
196	
197	  [I] Only shu reports the baseline itself.
198	- **W2. Label noise and leakage.** Exact-copy test-to-train leakage reaches 12.7% (BigVul) and 18.9% (CVEFixes) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. Benchmarks probably sit in LLM pre-training data [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 30] [A]. Only xiong and li2026llm test explicitly on post-cutoff code [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5]. shu adds a time split [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39].
199	- **W3. LLM-as-labeller.** li2026llm labels real-world warnings with Codex, a tool it also evaluates (94.36% accurate on 621 validated warnings) [@li2026llm, p. 11]. tan's LLM judge rates explanations higher in ways humans corroborate only for informativeness [@tan2026think, p. 8]. [I] Self-labelling can favour the labelling model.
200	- **W4. Unequal scoring between LLMs and SAST.** gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. CASTLE's LLM prompt states the reward and penalty scheme [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]. SAST tools run on default configurations [@gnieciak2025large, p. 8], and khare tests CodeQL only on synthetic data [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]. [I] These choices favour LLMs in two studies and SAST in one.
201	- **W5. Single runs, no statistics.** Most studies report one run of non-deterministic models without variance (§1). zhou2024's results rest on about 8–10 test CVEs per language [I] [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6]. xiong's real-world samples are 50 alerts each [@xiong2026sifting, p. 13]. shu chooses the best of ~30 configurations post hoc [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
202	- **W6. Little cost reporting.** Ten of 16 primary studies report no monetary cost (§1). Where cost is measured it is decisive: up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16].
203	- **W7. Narrow scope.** Data are C/C++-biased and long-tailed, and 555 mappable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 34]. 87 studies build custom datasets and only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. Only one of 40 detection studies to March 2024 worked at repository level [@zhou2025large, p. 18].
204	- **W8. Three-way comparisons are rare.** [I] Only khare evaluates LLMs, SAST and DL in one study, and its SAST arm covers synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]. zhou2024 compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST but no classic DL detector [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4].
205	- **W9. Preprint text vs version of record.** Fifteen published papers were analysed from arXiv copies (xiong2026sifting's copy is the formatted published article). du2026reducing comes from a v1 with a placeholder header [@du2026reducing, p. 2], so it has the highest risk that numbers changed. zhou2025large's only LLM-vs-SAST study is the authors' own zhou2024comparison [@zhou2025large, p. 22], so it is not independent support.
206	- **W10. Independence.** [I] guo and li2026llm share five C/C++ modules. ding, yildiz and tan share PrimeVul. Duplication figures reused elsewhere trace back to ding alone (critical review B).
207	
208	## 6. What this means for our research questions
209	
210	**RQ1 — effectiveness head-to-head.** No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale, general coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++) [@li2026llm, p. 7], but most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 11]. Against fine-tuned DL, the ranking depends on dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. **Strength: weak to moderate.** Results come from single-run studies with incompatible metrics and no pooling. The most robust pattern is "LLMs higher recall, lower precision" [I].
211	
212	**RQ2 — evaluation setups.** Setup explains much of the disagreement. Sources of variation:
213	- label noise (39–65% correct) [@risse2025top, p. 8];
214	- leakage [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4];
215	- balanced vs realistic class ratios [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7];
216	- synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5];
217	- function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8];
218	- custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].
219	
220	**Strength: moderate to strong**, consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs.
221	
222	**RQ3 — hybrids.** LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at under $0.20 per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]; **moderate**. Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12]. The gain depends on a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10]; **weak/contested**. Costs range from cents to $1,247.66 per project, against minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11] [A], and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9], which limits explainability.
223	
224	**RQ4 — CWEs, languages, scale.** LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs and worst on context-dependent, crypto/policy and memory-safety localisation [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]. CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. LLM performance falls with function or file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9]. Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. **Strength: weak.** Per-CWE cells are small and per-CWE results diverge across studies; for example, khare finds LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-476 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8], while ahmed reports over-flagging of it [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13].
225	
226	**RQ5 — open problems.** Recurring problems:
227	- verified, realistic, repository-level benchmarks with context [@zhou2025large, p. 19; @sheng2025llms, p. 25];
228	- same-benchmark three-way comparisons (W8);
229	- independent labelling and statistics (W3, W5);
230	- cost reporting (W6);
231	- contamination control (W2);
232	- true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19];
233	- workflow integration: none of 58 reviewed studies was integrated into developer workflows [@zhou2025large, p. 19].
234	
235	**Strength: moderate** as a description of recurring limitations. [I] These are candidate gaps only until the novelty checks in `gap-report.md` are run (standards §7).
236

# Research report: LLM-based vs traditional static analysis and deep learning for source-code vulnerability detection

- Project: `2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis`
- Date: 2026-11-12
- Based on: 20 full-text analyses, `evidence-matrix.md`, `reports/methodology-comparison.md`, `gap-report.md`, two critical reviews (A and B, 2026-11-12), `search/screening.md`, `search/search-log.md`.
- How to read the labels: **[V]** means we checked the number in the paper's own tables or results, **[A]** means the authors say it but we cannot check it, and **[I]** is our own interpretation. Unlabelled numbers are [V] from the cited page. Citations look like `[@key, p. N]`. The key is the paper's folder name and N is the PDF page.

## 1. Summary in plain language

We asked whether large language models (LLMs, such as GPT-4 or Claude) find security bugs in source code better than the two older approaches: rule-based scanners (SAST tools such as CodeQL) and neural networks trained on labelled vulnerable code (deep-learning or "DL" detectors). The short answer is that **no approach wins everywhere**. LLMs come out ahead on small, self-contained programs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]. CodeQL comes out ahead on synthetic test suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. On large real projects both families miss many bugs and raise many false alarms [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. The most consistent pattern [I] is that LLMs find more of the real bugs (higher recall) but also flag much more harmless code (lower precision). A large part of the disagreement between papers comes from **how** they test, not from the tools themselves. Studies differ in label quality, overlap between training and test data, the share of vulnerable samples, and how lenient the scoring is [@risse2025top, p. 8; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @gnieciak2025large, p. 6]. Combining the two, by letting an LLM filter a scanner's alarms, removes most false alarms cheaply but also throws away 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. For your comparative review, this "setup explains the contradictions" angle, applied across all three families, is the contribution we could not find in existing reviews (medium confidence).

## 2. What we did

- **Scope.** Source-code vulnerability detection by LLMs, SAST tools, DL detectors and LLM+SAST hybrids, published 2020–2026. Binary analysis, fuzzing and repair-only work were excluded (`RESEARCH.md`).
- **Searches.** Three search agents covered six facets: head-to-head LLM vs SAST, LLM vs DL, hybrids, evaluation realism, reasoning/agentic LLMs, and surveys. They ran about 19 searches on OpenAlex, Crossref and arXiv, plus *snowballing*, which means following the references and citations of central papers. Every search is logged in `search/search-log.md`, and every screening decision with its reason is in `search/screening.md`.
- **Included papers.** 20 papers in total:
  - 17 are published papers with a DOI.
  - IRIS [@li2024iris, p. 1] and RepoAudit [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 1] appeared at ICLR 2025 and ICML 2025. Both are peer-reviewed, but `rlab` records them as arXiv preprints because those venues issue no DOIs.
  - Only zhou2024comparison is a true preprint, meaning it is **not peer-reviewed** [@zhou2024comparison, p. 1].
  - Three of the 20 are reviews: kaniewski2026systematic, zhou2025large and sheng2025llms.
  - One candidate (VulnLLM-R) was dropped to keep to the 20-paper target, because it is a preprint with no venue.
- **Full text.** 20 of 20 papers were read in full and none were abstract-only (`rlab status`).
  - 18 PDFs were fetched automatically from legal open-access sources.
  - SecVulEval came from its arXiv preprint.
  - tan2026think came from a publisher PDF that you supplied.
  - 15 published papers were read from their arXiv versions, not the publisher's final text (the *version of record*). Numbers could differ slightly between the two (see §7).
- **Quality control.** Two independent critical reviews checked every analysis against the paper text and raised 36 findings, all of which were fixed. Most were small: labels, wording, or relative vs absolute percentages. None changed a paper's headline result.
- **Gap checks.** Before any gap was claimed we ran 26 targeted searches and 8 web searches (2026-11-12), as our standards require (`gap-report.md`).

## 3. Answers to the research questions

### RQ1 — Which family detects vulnerabilities better in head-to-head tests?

**Answer.** It depends on the setting:
- **Small, self-contained code.** Frontier LLMs beat SAST: macro F1 0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55 on ten C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10], and a CASTLE score of 977 for GPT-o3-mini vs 661 for the best non-LLM tool [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11].
- **Synthetic suites.** CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **Whole projects.** General coding agents reach much higher recall than SAST on C/C++ (59.55% vs 0–34.29%). Most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11].
- **Against fine-tuned DL.** The ranking depends on the dataset and on the share of vulnerable samples [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. On PrimeVul pairs of vulnerable and fixed code, every family scores near or below chance [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6].

**Evidence strength: weak to moderate.** The studies are mostly single runs, use five incompatible headline metrics, and cannot be pooled [I] (methodology comparison §3.5).

**What would change it.** A study that runs all three families on the same real, recent code with one shared metric (gap G2). Only khare2025understanding runs all three, and its SAST arm is on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7].

### RQ2 — How do evaluation setups differ, and do they explain the disagreements?

**Answer.** Yes, to a large extent. The main sources of variation are:
- **Wrong labels.** Only 39–65% of "vulnerable" labels in popular datasets are correct [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- **Test data copied from training data.** Up to 18.9% exact copies [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4].
- **Balanced vs realistic test sets.** The class balance flips rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40]. LLM F1 falls from about 49–65% to 5.41–12.21% when pairs are dropped [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- **Synthetic vs real code.** LLM accuracy is 10.5% lower on real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5].
- **Function-level vs line-level scoring.** Line-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8].
- **Custom datasets with inconsistent splits** [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35].

Even a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11], so high scores on that dataset say little about real understanding.

**Evidence strength: moderate to strong.** Independent primary studies agree, and two systematic reviews concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20].

**What would change it.** A controlled study showing that rankings stay stable across clean and noisy versions of the same benchmark.

**Answer.** It depends on the type of hybrid.

- **LLM as alarm filter.** This is the most consistent benefit in the corpus, but it is a trade-off.
  - An industrial study removes 94–98% of false alarms while keeping 75–88% of real bugs, at a few cents per alarm [@du2026reducing, p. 8]. This is the authors' own method at Tencent, and it covers general bug types, not only security bugs.
  - An agent study cuts the false-positive rate on OWASP from 98.3% to 6.3% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12] but misses 22.25% of real vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18].
  - **Strength: moderate.**
- **LLM inside the analyser** (IRIS, RepoAudit). The tool authors' own evaluations look strong:
  - IRIS found 55 of 120 Java CVEs vs CodeQL's 27 [@li2024iris, p. 8].
  - RepoAudit reports 78.43% precision [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 8].

  An independent project-scale study does not reproduce these gains [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12]. IRIS's gain also depends on GPT-4, and smaller LLMs make it worse [@li2024iris, p. 10]. **Strength: weak and contested.**
- **Cost.** LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 for one project, while SAST takes minutes with no token cost [@li2026llm, p. 16].
- **Explainability.** LLMs sometimes point at the wrong location [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11] [A], and a fluent explanation does not mean the verdict is correct [@tan2026think, p. 9].

**What would change it.** An independent, blinded replication of IRIS or RepoAudit (gap G4). For filtering, results on real security alerts rather than the synthetic OWASP suite (gap G3).

**Answer.**
- **By vulnerability type.** LLMs do best on self-contained injection-type weaknesses. They do worst on weaknesses that depend on wider context or on cryptography policy, and on locating memory-safety bugs [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]. For example, the filtering agent misses only 0.41–2.38% of injection bugs but 77.17–84.50% of weak-crypto and weak-hash bugs [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18]. - **By code size.** LLM performance drops as functions or files get longer [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9].
- **By language.** Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28].

- same-benchmark three-family comparisons;
- independent human labelling and statistical testing [@li2026llm, p. 11];
- cost reporting;
- control of *contamination*, i.e. test code that the LLM already saw during training;
- limiting the loss of real bugs during filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19];
